title: Aristotelian Othello
welcome_lead: Map Aristotle's tragic categories onto Othello — hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, catharsis.
meta_desc: Aristotelian conventions applied to AQA Othello at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have set Othello on the Aristotelian terrace — every category present, sharpened by modern critique.

concepts.def: Othello's tragic flaw — credulity, jealousy or a militarised honour code, depending on critical reading.
The handkerchief scene and III.iii together flip Othello from devoted husband to obsessed avenger.
Othello's recognition of Iago's deception in Act V, after Desdemona's death.
The audience's purgation of pity (for Othello and Desdemona) and fear (for the fragility of trust).
The audience knows of Iago's plot from his soliloquies long before Othello does — sustained tragic tension.
Lodovico and the Venetian state reimpose order; Iago is led off to torture, Othello and Desdemona are dead.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Critics differ on the central flaw. F. R. Leavis saw Othello's self-dramatising egotism as the engine; A. C. Bradley emphasised his noble nature deceived.

Modern critics often add race, class and military culture to the answer.

The temptation scene is the play's peripeteia. Iago's hints, the handkerchief and Othello's escalating jealousy drive the reversal.

The scene's length and density of staged emotion make it one of the great Shakespearean set pieces.
Act V delivers anagnorisis (Othello realises Iago lied), catastrophe (the murder of Desdemona, Othello's suicide), and ritual closure (Lodovico's verdict on Iago).
